title: Wedge Pop
teaches: The Wedge Pop as we trade it: a stock that corrected under its short averages rests a few tight days under them, then trades through the base's high and closes back above them on more volume. We buy at market through the pivot, no more than 4% past it, above the 200-day, with the stop a few cents under the pop day's low; the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.

questions.q: In one line, what is a Wedge Pop?
choices: A break up from a base under the EMAs
A bounce off a crash low itself
A pole that doubles in a few weeks
A cross back over the EMAs with no base
questions.answer: A break up from a base under the EMAs
questions.why: A break up from a base under the EMAs, the short exponential averages. After a sharp rebound off the low, the stock rests under them. The pop is the first rally back through them, and Deepvue says the same. A bare cross is not enough: it needs the tight base and the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: A stock rests under its averages, the bars get small, then it pops back through them.

wrong.A bounce off a crash low itself: The bounce is the Reversal Extension, which comes before. The pop comes after the stock rests under its short averages and clears them.
wrong.A pole that doubles in a few weeks: The pop is not about a fast doubling. It comes after a rebound and a tight base under the averages.
wrong.A cross back over the EMAs with no base: A cross alone is not a pop. It needs the tight base and the pivot.

questions.simple: A Wedge Pop is a stock rising back through its short averages after resting in a tight base under them.

reasons: a stable definition on two agreeing Tier 2 publishers

questions.q: On a Wedge Pop the stop goes a few cents under the pop day's low.
questions.why: True. The stop sits a few cents under the pop day's low, not exactly on it. We set the stop first and size the trade from it. Kell did the same on CAVA, with a stop set under the day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the pop day's low.
questions.simple: True. The stop goes a few cents under the pop day's low, not exactly on it, and the share size comes from it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and F62
the card keeps the pop day's low as the default under D-008

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.why: 4%. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and on a Wedge Pop that point is the pivot. A pop day that runs further is a chase. Wait for the first tight day or a pullback. Chasing costs size, not risk, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent past the pivot and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.
questions.sentence: No buy more than ___% past the pivot.
questions.simple: 4%, because past that you are chasing, and the stop stays put, so the extra distance means fewer shares.

deeper.trap: Trap: buying the close of a big pop day. If the day runs more than 4% past the pivot, it is a chase. Wait for a tight day or a pullback.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C28

questions.q: Which pair of averages does Kell's cycle of price revolve around?
questions.why: The 10-day and 20-day EMAs. Kell's cycle revolves around them, and they guide the intermediate trend. The 50 and 200-day simple averages track the longer trend. We name the 10 and 20 here only as Kell's own pair. We use the 9 and 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Kell's cycle lives on two short exponential averages. The slow lines are for the bigger trend.

wrong.The 50 and 200-day SMAs: Those track the longer trend, per the same pages. Kell's cycle revolves around the 10 and 20-day EMAs.
wrong.The 20 and 100-day SMAs: Kell's pages name the 10 and 20-day EMAs for the cycle and the 50 and 200 for the longer trend. A 100-day line is in neither pair.
wrong.The 8 and 21-day EMAs: That is not Kell's pair. His cycle pages name the 10 and 20-day EMAs.

questions.simple: Kell's cycle runs on the 10 and 20-day EMAs. The 50 and 200-day averages track the longer trend instead.

reasons: the averages pair is a held decision, D-021

questions.q: A close back above the averages is enough to call a Wedge Pop.
questions.why: False. Many traders mistakenly believe the Wedge Pop is simply about crossing the moving averages. Kell says to focus on price bars and volume instead. A cross alone is not a pop: it needs the tight base and the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: A cross is not a pop. First the tight base, then the trade through its high.
questions.simple: False. Crossing back above the averages is not enough, because a real pop also needs a tight base and a trade through its high.

deeper.trap: Trap: buying the cross. A wide, loose rebound through the averages with no tight base is a remount, not a Wedge Pop.

reasons: rests on the criteria card (house)

questions.q: On a Wedge Pop, what is the pivot?
choices: The highest high of the base
The low of the Reversal Extension
questions.answer: The highest high of the base
questions.why: The highest high of the base, the short-term resistance. A tight price range near short-term resistance makes the tradable pivot, and the Wedge Pop is the trade through it. The pivot is not the Reversal Extension's low, not the 200-day line, and not the pop day's closing price.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the base's high before the open. That is the line it must trade through.

wrong.The 200-day moving average: The 200-day is a line the stock must be above. It is not the buy point.
wrong.The low of the Reversal Extension: That low marks the bottom. The pivot is the top of the base that forms after it.
wrong.The pop day's closing price: The close comes after the buy. The pivot is set before the pop day.

questions.simple: The pivot is the highest price of the base, the line the stock must trade through for the pop to start.

reasons: a stable definition with three agreeing facts

questions.story: The day before the pop.

questions.q: We buy a Wedge Pop with a market order as it trades through the pivot, in regular hours.
questions.why: True. The buy is a market order as the stock trades through the pivot, in regular hours only. Entries are market orders, and we make no new buys outside regular trading hours.
questions.lesson_line: Set the alert at the pivot. When it trades through, buy at market.
questions.simple: True. We buy at market the moment it trades through the pivot, and only in regular hours.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E57 and E58
the intraday trigger 'as it trades through the pivot' is a held decision, D-003

questions.q: Once the pop works, we add more shares at each new range.
questions.why: False. We put the full size on at one price with one stop, with no adding on the way up. Kell adds as each new range breaks, but that is his method, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: One entry, one stop. The size goes on once.
questions.simple: False. We buy the full size once, at one price with one stop, even though Kell adds at new ranges.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A5 and differs from Kell

questions.q: In Kell's words, what does a Wedge Pop signal?
choices: A bottom and a new uptrend
questions.answer: A bottom and a new uptrend
questions.why: A bottom and a new uptrend. Kell's page says the Wedge Pop signals that a stock has bottomed and is starting a new uptrend. His QQQ pop confirmed the low that way. It signals the turn. It does not promise how far the move runs.
questions.lesson_line: Kell reads a Wedge Pop as a stock that has bottomed and is starting a new uptrend.

wrong.A top and new downtrend: That is the Wedge Drop, the mirror. The pop starts an up-cycle.
wrong.A pause in a downtrend: A pause under the averages is the base that comes before the pop. The pop is the break out of it, and Kell says it signals a bottom.
wrong.A gap it must fill: The pop signals a turn, not a gap to fill. Kell says most powerful pops start with gaps.

questions.simple: Kell says a Wedge Pop signals that a stock has bottomed and is starting a new uptrend.

reasons: whether a Reversal Extension must come first is a held decision, D-077

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.why: 3. The base needs at least 3 sessions after the low. At least half the closes sit at or under the higher of the 10 and 20-day EMAs. A stock needs a few days to retreat before a lasting bottom. Three is a floor, not a target.
questions.lesson_line: No base, no pop. A few quiet days under the averages come first.
questions.sentence: The shortest base we allow runs ___ sessions after the low.
questions.simple: The base must run at least three sessions after the low, because a stock needs a few days to retreat.

reasons: the number is the proposed card's minimum

questions.q: Volume drying up through the base counts in the setup's favor.
questions.why: True. Volume drying up through the base is a strong cue on our card: distribution volume decreasing before accumulation picks up. Kell's first two QQQ pops failed with no increase in accumulation and consistent distribution volume. A quiet base helps. The trigger is still the trade through the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet volume in the base, loud volume on the pop. That is the picture.
questions.simple: Yes, quiet volume in the base is a strong cue because selling is fading before buyers step in.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's A+ cue

questions.q: A stock gaps up over the pivot, through both averages. What does the gap tell us?
choices: Weakness; the gap will soon fill in
Strength, but too late to buy now
Nothing; gaps are only noise here
questions.why: Strength. Kell: most Wedge Pops that lead to new, powerful trends start with gaps. Our card calls a gap up through the pivot and the averages the A+ pop, and a gap up to 4% past the pivot is still a buy. RCL in 2009 was a gap open under the 4% chase line. In our scan a gap open of 1% or more did better, not worse.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the averages is strength, not a reason to wait.

wrong.Weakness; the gap will soon fill in: Waiting for a fill is a guess. In our scan a gap open of 1% or more did better, not worse.
wrong.Strength, but too late to buy now: A gap up to 4% past the pivot is still inside the chase line, so it is not too late.
wrong.Nothing; gaps are only noise here: It matters: our card calls a gap up through the pivot and the averages the A+ pop.

questions.simple: A gap up through the pivot shows strength, so we buy the open unless it is more than 4% past the pivot.

reasons: the 4% chase line is the owner's rulebook (C28)
the gap row is on the proposed card

questions.story: The day before the pop.

questions.q: The first pullback into the rising averages after the pop is a separate setup, the EMA Crossback.
questions.why: True. The first pullback into the rising averages after the pop is the EMA Crossback. It is a separate setup and a new trade, not an add. Kell names a pop first, then a Crossback taking place after it.
questions.lesson_line: Pop first, crossback second. Two setups, two trades.
questions.simple: True. The first pullback after the pop is the EMA Crossback, which is its own setup and a new trade.

reasons: rests on the criteria card (house)

questions.q: After the pop, which close says the pop failed?
choices: A close under the pop day's low
A red day somewhere in the next week
A close under the pop day's open
questions.answer: A close under the pop day's low
questions.why: A close under the pop day's low. Our card says that close means the pop failed. The stop sits just under that low anyway. Kell: if it fails, cut losses quickly. The 200-day line decides whether we buy at all, not whether the pop failed.
questions.lesson_line: The pop day's low is the line. Under it, the pop is done.

wrong.A close under the 200-day average: The 200-day line decides whether we buy at all. It is not the failure line.
wrong.A red day somewhere in the next week: A red day can still hold above the pop day's low. Noise is not a failure.
wrong.A close under the pop day's open: A close under the open can still sit above the pop day's low. The failure line is the low.

questions.simple: The pop failed if it closes under the pop day's low, which is where our stop already sits, just below.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's failure row
fixed before

questions.q: A $12 stock that trades $15 million a day passes our liquidity rule.
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day, on the 50-day average. This stock clears the price test at $12 but misses the dollar test at $15 million.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars and twenty million a day, or it is not on the list.
questions.simple: False. The stock passes on price, but it trades only $15 million a day and we need at least $20 million.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B23

questions.q: The last 5 sessions averaged a 2.10 range; the 10 before averaged 3.00. What is the last 5 divided by the 10 before?
questions.why: 0.70. Divide the last 5 sessions' average range by the average range of the 10 before: 2.10 / 3.00 = 0.70. Our card wants a ratio under 0.85, so this base is tightening.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the shrink. Do not eyeball it.
questions.simple: 0.70, found by dividing 2.10 by 3.00. That is under 0.85, so the ranges are shrinking.

deeper.trap: Trap: eyeballing the shrink. Measure it: the last 5 sessions' average range over the 10 before. Our card wants it under 0.85.

reasons: a computed key
the 0.85 cut-off is a proposed criterion on the card

wrong.1.43x: Flipped it: the 10 before divided by the last 5.
wrong.0.50x: Divided the session counts, 5 by 10, not the ranges.
wrong.0.30x: That is the shrink, one minus 0.70, not the ratio.

questions.q: The pop day ran 100.00 to 106.00 and closed at 104.00. Where did it close, in percent of its range from the low?
questions.why: 66.7%. The close above the low is 104 - 100. The range is 106 - 100. So (104 - 100) / (106 - 100) x 100 = 66.7%. Our card wants the pop day to close in the top 40% of its range, so this passes. The close is known only at the close, so it grades the pop.
questions.lesson_line: Where the pop closes grades it. Near the high is what you want.
questions.simple: 66.7%, found as the close minus the low over the day's range. That is inside the top 40%, so it passes.

reasons: a computed key
the top-40% cut-off is a proposed criterion on the card

wrong.98.1%: Divided the close by the high. That ignores the low.
wrong.33.3%: Measured down from the high instead of up from the low.
wrong.3.8%: Divided by the close, not by the day's range.

questions.q: Bought at 175.52 with the stop at 171.31. Where is 3R?
questions.why: $188.15. One R is the fill minus the stop: 175.52 - 171.31. Add three of those to the fill: 175.52 + 3 x (175.52 - 171.31) = 188.15. 3R is a measuring stick, not an order to sell. STLD took six sessions to reach it. The first sell is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, not a sell order.
questions.simple: 188.15 is the fill plus three times the gap between the fill and the stop. It is a measuring stick, not a sell order.

deeper.example: STLD, March 2026, was this very trade: bought at 175.52 with the stop at 171.31. 3R took six sessions, then the stock ran from 175 to 280 in ten weeks.

reasons: a computed key
the first sell is the owner's D-013 judgment, not a fixed 3R sale

wrong.$192.36: Added four R, counting the fill as the first one.
wrong.$196.57: Used five R, the far end of the breakeven window.
wrong.$200.78: Doubled the three R to six R.

questions.story: Bought on the pop.

questions.q: When does our first sell usually come on a pop?
choices: Day 3 at the earliest, or later
Day 1, to lock in a quick gain
Never; hold it all to the end
questions.answer: Day 3 at the earliest, or later
questions.why: Day 3 at the earliest, and often later. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. FNV was up 3R the next session, and that is still rarely the day to sell. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Rarely sell on day 1. Day 3 at the earliest, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push.

wrong.Day 1, to lock in a quick gain: We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.At exactly 3R, whatever the day: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
wrong.Never; hold it all to the end: We do sell. The first sell is a judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push.

questions.simple: We rarely sell on day 1. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest, often into a longer push.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (the first sell is a judgment)

questions.story: Bought on the pop at 45.53 with the stop at 44.77. By the next session it is already up 3R.

questions.q: By our default, the stop moves to breakeven as soon as the trade is up 1R.
questions.why: False. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, so the stop does not move at 1R. It only ever moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. Then a stop-out costs about nothing.
questions.simple: False. Breakeven starts at 2R, not at 1R.

deeper.trap: Trap: moving the stop to breakeven at the first sign of profit. The card starts breakeven at 2R, not sooner.

reasons: the breakeven range comes from the card

questions.q: How do we trail what is left on a fast mover?
questions.why: A close under the 9 EMA. We trail the 9 EMA for fast movers and the 20 EMA for steadier ones. We sell what is left on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: Fast movers ride the 9 EMA. Steady ones get the 20 EMA.

wrong.A fixed 8% under the high: Our trail is an average with a close below it, not a fixed percent.
wrong.A close under the 50-day: Not our trail. Ours is the 9 EMA for fast movers and the 20 EMA for steadier ones.
wrong.A close under the 20 EMA: That is the trail for steadier movers. Fast movers get the 9 EMA.

questions.simple: A close under the 9 EMA, because the rule gives fast movers the 9 EMA trail and we sell on a close below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E52

questions.q: A pop still under 1R is given 20 trading days before it is sold.
questions.why: False. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. It is not given 20. In our scan the median winner reached 3R in 3 sessions, far faster than 10 days.
questions.lesson_line: Good pops move fast. Ten days and nothing, the money goes elsewhere.
questions.simple: False. We sell a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days, not 20, so the money can go elsewhere.

deeper.trap: Trap: waiting for a slow one to come good. The rule frees the money after 10 days. The median winner in our scan took 3 sessions to reach 3R. The slowest of our ten examples took seven, CROX.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C33

questions.q: Buy now, or wait?
choices: Wait for a tight day or pullback
Wait for a higher close, then buy
Buy now, it is strong and moving up
Buy half size now just to be in
questions.answer: Wait for a tight day or pullback
questions.why: Wait. 42.00 is more than 4% past the 40.00 pivot, and we never buy more than 4% above the buy point. A pop day that runs further is a chase. Wait for the first tight day or pullback after it. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays put, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss the pop than chase it. The tight day after it is the next door.

wrong.Wait for a higher close, then buy: A higher close is even farther past the pivot. The 4% line only gets farther away.
wrong.Buy now, it is strong and moving up: Strong and too far away are both true. The line is 4% past the pivot.
wrong.Buy half size now just to be in: Half of a chase is still a chase.

questions.story: The pivot is 40.00. You missed the first move. At 11:00 the stock trades 42.00 after one wide bar.
questions.simple: Wait, because the price is more than 4% past the pivot, which makes a buy now a chase.

reasons: the 4% chase line is the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.q: Your fill would be 55.40. The 9 EMA is 50.00. How far above it, in percent?
questions.why: 10.8%. The fill is above the average by (55.40 - 50.00) / 50.00 = 10.8%. We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA. It is too stretched to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Read the stretch in percent before you buy. Past 10% over the 9 EMA, I pass.
questions.simple: 10.8%, which is past the 10% limit above the 9 EMA, so the stock is too stretched and we skip it.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook C29

wrong.9.7%: Divided by the fill, not the average. That lands under the limit and wrongly lets the buy through.
wrong.5.4%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.1.08%: A decimal slip, one place too far left.

questions.q: Fill 24.58, stop 23.68. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 3.66%. The stop's distance is the gap over the fill: (24.58 - 23.68) / 24.58 x 100 = 3.66%. Our stop usually sits within about 3%. Wider than that, the card says a smaller position or a pass, never a tighter stop to fit. This is CROX in 2007, the widest stop of our ten.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: 3.66%, a bit wider than our usual 3%. The card then says a smaller size or a pass, never a tighter stop.

deeper.trap: Trap: tightening the stop so the trade fits. The card says never. A stop that has to be 8% or more away is B- at best.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook A13

wrong.3.80%: Divided by the stop, not by the fill.
wrong.0.90%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.36.6%: A decimal slip. The stop is a few percent away, not a third.

questions.story: Bought on the pop.

questions.q: Account 200,000. Risk 0.25%. Fill 181.80, stop 179.58. How many shares?
questions.why: 225 shares. Dollars at risk are 200,000 x 0.25%. Risk per share is the fill minus the stop: 181.80 - 179.58. Divide the first by the second and round down to 225. The position cap can still shrink it. A risk of 0.25% is the low end for B- or lower setups.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk, divided by the distance to the stop, rounded down, is the share count.
questions.simple: 225 shares, because the dollars at risk divided by the gap between the fill and the stop give 225 after rounding down.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook A5

wrong.2,252 shares: Typed the risk as ten times too big, so the share count came out ten times too big.
wrong.1,100 shares: Divided the account by the price and ignored the stop.
wrong.409 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the stop's percent, not by the dollars per share.

questions.story: Bought on the pop.

questions.q: Buy?
choices: No, a report is too close
No, it needs a gap up
questions.answer: No, a report is too close
questions.why: No. We take no new buy in the 3 days before an earnings report, and this one comes out tonight. The chart is not the question. MU in March 2022 popped, reported that evening, and the next day's low of 78.60 went through the 79.21 stop.
questions.lesson_line: Check the calendar before the chart. A report inside three days and I wait.

wrong.Yes, the setup is done: A complete setup still waits for the calendar. No new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Size does not fix it. The rule is no new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.No, it needs a gap up: A gap helps, but a pop does not need one. The reason to wait here is the report.

questions.story: The chart ends the day before. Today the stock trades through its pivot, 81.20, on 1.8 times the 50-day volume, above both averages. The company's earnings come out after today's close.
questions.simple: No, because we take no new buy in the three days before an earnings report, however good the chart looks.

reasons: the 3-day window is the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: How do you enter this pop?
choices: Buy half now, half on a dip
questions.why: Buy the open at market. If a stock opens above the pivot, we buy at the open when the gap is no more than 4% above it. 13.18 is inside that line. A gap up through the pivot and the averages is the A+ pop. The stop still goes a few cents under the day's low.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the pivot inside the chase line is the A+ pop. Buy it.

wrong.Pass, gaps tend to fill: Kell says most of the powerful pops start with gaps. On our card a gap up through the pivot is the A+ pop.
wrong.Buy half now, half on a dip: We put the full size on at one price with one stop. No adding.
wrong.Wait for a dip to 12.95: The rule is to buy the open when the gap is within 4% of the pivot. Waiting for a pullback is for a pop that runs past 4%.

questions.story: The chart ends the day before. The base's high, the pivot, is 12.95. On the pop day the stock opens at 13.18, above both averages.
questions.simple: Buy the open at market, because 13.18 is a gap within 4% of the 12.95 pivot.

deeper.example: RCL, pop 2009-07-15: it gapped open above the 12.95 pivot, under the 4% chase line. We buy the open at 13.18. The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, at 12.97, above the pivot.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C28 and E57

questions.q: It gaps over the pivot and you buy the open. Where does the stop go?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
Exactly at the day's low price
At the open price, right at the entry
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it. The low of day is the primary stop. The pattern's low or a line minus a cushion can also work, but they are not the main stop. On a gap the day's low can sit above the pivot, as it did for RCL in 2009. The stop follows that low. The 200-day line decides whether we buy at all.
questions.lesson_line: The stop follows the day's low, wherever the gap puts it.

wrong.Exactly at the day's low price: Our rule puts the stop a few cents under the low, not on it.
wrong.Under the 200-day moving average: The 200-day line decides whether we buy at all. It is the gate, not the main stop.
wrong.At the open price, right at the entry: A stop on the entry price gives the trade no room. Breakeven comes later, after the trade has worked.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under the day's low, even after a gap, because the stop follows that low.

reasons: the stop default is the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)
the base-low option is held (D-008)

questions.story: The chart ends the day before the pop.

questions.q: The stock trades 1,500,000 shares a day on average. Our volume ceiling on the position?
questions.why: 15,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 1,500,000 is 15,000. The ceiling holds whatever the stop is. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.150,000 shares: That is ten times our ceiling. The limit is 1% of the average daily volume.
wrong.1,500 shares: That is a tenth of the ceiling. The limit is 1% of the volume, not a fraction of that.
wrong.30,000 shares: That is double the ceiling. The limit is 1% of the volume.

questions.simple: 15,000 shares is 1% of the 1,500,000 average daily volume, which is the most we ever own.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook D42

questions.q: Which setup is this?
questions.why: An EMA Crossback. A crossback is the first pullback into averages the stock already rides, within 20 sessions after a pop. A Wedge Pop comes after a correction spent mostly under the averages. This stock has held above the 20 EMA since its pop. DECK was a near-miss of this kind: a pullback inside an uptrend.
questions.lesson_line: Ask where the stock came from. Up from under the averages is a pop; down into them is a crossback.

wrong.Wedge Pop: A pop is the push up through the averages from under them. This stock has been riding above them.
wrong.A flat base breakout: The story shows no flat box under a flat top. The stock already popped and is dipping back to its average.
wrong.A remount setup: A remount retakes a line lost for 5 or more closes with one wide candle. This stock has held its 20 EMA every close since the pop.

questions.story: Fourteen sessions ago the stock popped back over its averages. Every close since held above the 20 EMA. Today it dips to the average for the first time and holds.
questions.simple: It is a crossback, because the stock already rides above its averages and is dipping into them, not rising from under them.

reasons: the prior-decline test is a held decision, D-077

questions.q: Is this a Wedge Pop?
choices: No, a cross with no base or pivot
Yes, if the volume is heavy
questions.answer: No, a cross with no base or pivot
questions.why: No. A cross of the averages alone is not a Wedge Pop: it needs the tight base and the pivot. Kell: focus on price bars and volume.
questions.lesson_line: No tight base, no pivot, no pop. A cross is just a cross.

wrong.Yes, it reclaimed both averages: Reclaiming the averages is one part. Without the tight base there is no pivot to trade through.
wrong.Yes, if the volume is heavy: Volume grades a real pop. It cannot make a pop out of a ragged range.

questions.story: Price closed over both averages today. The two weeks before were wide and ragged, with no clear high to trade through.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
choices: Take it, the base is clean
Take it, but at half size
Pass, the base is too short
questions.why: Pass. For a stock, no longs below the 200-day simple moving average. The one exception is indexes and ETFs built to magnify an index's moves, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. This is a stock. That January 2019 pop closed 7.3% under the 200-day, and the stock went higher without us. A clean base or a smaller size does not change a hard rule.
questions.lesson_line: A pop that works is not always our pop. Under the 200-day, I pass.

wrong.Take it, the base is clean: A clean base under the 200-day is still under the 200-day. That rule is hard.
wrong.Take it, but at half size: A hard rule has no half size. Under the 200-day there is no long.
wrong.Pass, the base is too short: A 6-day base is longer than the 3-session minimum on our card. The base was fine. The 200-day line is the problem.

questions.story: The chart ends the day before the pop. A January 2019 chart: a 36% decline, a 6-day base, and a pop on 1.1x the base's volume. The pop day closed 7.3% under the 200-day.
questions.simple: Pass, because our hard rule bars stock longs below the 200-day line, even when the base is clean and the pop works.

reasons: a hard rule in the owner's rulebook (B26)
the index and ETF option is held (D-009)

questions.q: Is this a Wedge Pop by our card?
choices: Yes, but light volume lowers the grade
No, light volume ends it right there
No, a 6-day base is too short to count
Yes, and it is a top grade A+ pop
questions.answer: Yes, but light volume lowers the grade
questions.why: Yes, it is still a Wedge Pop. Volume raises the grade, but it is not a requirement for the setup to count. This one closed above both averages out of a tight base, on 0.88 times the base days' volume, so it grades lower. Kell's first two QQQ pops failed with no increase in accumulation, so a light pop is a weaker picture.
questions.lesson_line: Volume raises the grade. A light pop is weaker, not ruled out.

wrong.No, light volume ends it right there: Light volume does not end it. Volume raises the grade; it is not a requirement for the setup to count. This one grades lower.
wrong.No, a 6-day base is too short to count: The story gives a 6-day base, past the 3-session minimum. The base was fine.
wrong.Yes, and it is a top grade A+ pop: The strongest pop comes on clearly more volume than the base days. This light volume holds the grade back.

questions.story: An 18% decline, then a 6-day tight base. It trades through the pivot and closes above both averages, on 0.88x the base days' volume.
questions.simple: Yes, it still counts as a pop, because volume only raises the grade, and this light volume lowers it.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's no-volume row
volume rules are a held decision (D-006)

questions.q: Two pop days: one closes near its high, one closes back under the pivot. Which is stronger?
choices: The one with the wider range
questions.why: The close near the high. Our card wants the pop day to close above both averages and the pivot, in the top 40% of its range. In our scan a close back under the pivot on the pop day did far worse. The share reaching three R fell to 23.1%, against 46.5% for a close above it. That was the strongest single cut. The close is known only at the close, so it can only confirm the pop afterwards.
questions.lesson_line: A pop that closes near its high is stronger than one that fades back under the pivot.

wrong.The close under the pivot: A close back under the pivot did much worse in our scan.
wrong.They are equally strong: They are not equal. A close back under the pivot cut the share reaching three R to 23.1% from 46.5%.
wrong.The one with the wider range: A wide bar is not the test. Where it closes counts: above both averages and the pivot, in the top 40% of its range.

questions.simple: The close near the high is stronger, since a close back under the pivot did much worse in our scan.

deeper.counter: A strong close does not guarantee a winner. In our examples four pops were stopped out, and all four pop days closed at or near the high and above both averages. Nothing on the pop day's candle separated them from the winners. The close helps us read the pop; the stop protects us when it still fails.

reasons: rests on our scan figures and the proposed card
fixed before

questions.q: A close back under both averages and inside the base, within 5 sessions of the pop, invalidates it.
questions.why: True. A close back under both averages and back inside the base within 5 sessions ends it. That is the failure mode. The pop fades back under the pivot or both averages within days. It is usually on no rise in volume, and the next session takes the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A real pop holds its ground. Back in the base means the pop is gone.
questions.simple: True, because a close back under both averages and inside the base within five sessions means the pop has faded.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's invalidation row
fixed before

questions.q: Buy it?
questions.why: No. The index still making lower lows with its averages falling invalidates the buy on our card. Kell avoided long swings until the index showed a major capitulation reversal extension or switched to a buy signal. Strength in one stock does not change that, and a tighter stop only gets tagged sooner.
questions.lesson_line: A pop against a falling market is swimming upstream. Let the index turn first.

wrong.Yes, the stock is strong: Strength in one stock does not stop a falling market from dragging it down.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop: A tighter stop than the rule only gets tagged sooner. The issue is the market, not the stop.
wrong.No, it must clear the 50-day: Reclaiming the 50-day makes an A+ pop but is not required. The reason to wait here is the falling index.

questions.story: Your stock pops cleanly through its pivot. The index is still making lower lows, its averages pointing down.
questions.simple: No, because the index is still making lower lows with falling averages, so we wait even if the stock looks strong.

reasons: rests on the proposed card, which lists a falling index as both a no-buy and a B- cue

questions.q: What changes?
choices: Move the stop to the pivot
questions.why: The size, not the stop. The honest stop is 3.66% away, wider than about 3%. Then take a smaller position or skip. Never tighten the stop to fit. The size comes from the stop. CROX had the widest stop of our ten winners and still worked.
questions.lesson_line: Never shrink the stop to fit the size. Shrink the size to fit the stop.

wrong.Pull the stop in to 3%: The stop never gets tighter to fit. It sits a few cents under the day's low.
wrong.Nothing, size as normal: A stop wider than about 3% means a smaller position or a pass.
wrong.Move the stop to the pivot: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low. Moving it to fit is the mistake.

questions.story: Bought on the pop at 24.58. The stop sits a few cents under the pop day's low, at 23.68, which is 3.66% away.
questions.simple: Make the position smaller, because the stop is 3.66% away, wider than about 3%, and we never tighten a stop to fit.

reasons: the 3% line is the owner's rulebook (A13)

questions.q: Same base, two pop days: one on 1.2 times the base days' volume, one on 2.5 times with a gap up. Which is stronger?
questions.why: The gap up on 2.5 times. The strongest pop gaps up through the averages and the pivot on clearly more volume than the base days. STLD popped on only 1.2 times the base's volume, the lightest of our ten, and still worked. A light pop can work, but it is the weaker picture.
questions.lesson_line: More volume and a gap make a stronger pop. Light volume makes it weaker.

wrong.The pop on 1.2 times: Less volume and no gap is the weaker picture. The strongest pop gaps up on clearly more volume than the base days.
wrong.They tie in strength: They are not equal. The strongest pop gaps up through the pivot on clearly more volume than the base days.
wrong.Neither, it is a chase: A gap is not a chase by itself. We buy the open when the gap is no more than 4% above the pivot.

questions.simple: The gap on 2.5 times volume is stronger, because the best pop gaps through the pivot on more volume than the base.

deeper.example: STLD in March 2026 is the light-volume case: a 7-day base, a pop on 1.2 times the base's volume, buy 175.52, stop 171.31. The first 3R took six sessions, then it ran from 175 to 280 in ten weeks. Light volume made it the weaker picture. It did not stop it working.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's A+ row
volume rules are a held decision (D-006)

questions.q: By our card, which is the stronger pop?
choices: Pop A, early in the cycle
Pop B, the trend is proven
Pop B, it has more bases behind it
questions.answer: Pop A, early in the cycle
questions.why: Pop A. Early in a new cycle beats the fourth base of an old one. A late-cycle base counts against the pop. DHI popped three sessions after SPY's 2023 low.
questions.lesson_line: Early pops in a new cycle are the best ones. Late bases in old trends are tired.

wrong.Pop B, the trend is proven: Our card wants early in a new cycle, not the fourth base of an old one. A late-cycle base counts against the pop.
wrong.They are about equally strong: They are not equal. Early in a new cycle beats the fourth base of an old one.
wrong.Pop B, it has more bases behind it: More bases is not more proof. The fourth base of an old trend is late in the cycle, and that counts against the pop.

questions.story: Pop A comes three sessions after the index's own low. Pop B comes in the index's fourth month up, on the stock's fourth base.
questions.simple: Pop A is stronger, because a pop early in a new cycle beats the fourth base of an old trend.

reasons: rests on the proposed early-cycle row
market timing is a held decision (D-018)

questions.q: How does that read?
choices: Stronger: the gap will fill up
Same: only the pivot break counts
questions.why: Weaker. Overhead supply right above the pivot is a weak cue on our card. An unfilled gap down or a falling 50-day just over it are examples. Reclaiming the 50-day too makes it stronger. Kell's TSLA rejected at its gap resistance the day after its pop, and he played defense.
questions.lesson_line: Look up before you buy. Sellers waiting just overhead cap the pop.

wrong.Stronger: it cleared the pivot: Clearing the pivot is only the start. Sellers just overhead cap the move.
wrong.Stronger: the gap will fill up: Our card reads an unfilled gap down right above the pivot as overhead supply, a weak cue. It is a ceiling to clear, not a lift.
wrong.Same: only the pivot break counts: Our card treats overhead supply right above the pivot as a weak cue, so the break alone is not the whole read.

questions.story: The pop clears the pivot. Right above it sits an unfilled gap down, and the 50-day is falling just overhead.
questions.simple: It reads weaker, because an unfilled gap down and a falling 50-day sit right overhead and sellers there cap the pop.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's grade row

questions.q: The market reading is Orange. A clean B pop and an A+ gap pop set up. What do we buy?
choices: Just the A+ pop, not the B
questions.answer: Just the A+ pop, not the B
questions.why: Just the A+ gap pop. Orange takes only A+ setups, so the B pop waits for a better market. The reading is a guide.
questions.lesson_line: The market sets how many pops I take, and which ones.

wrong.Both, each at full size: Full risk is for a Green market. Orange takes only A+ setups.
wrong.Both, each at half size: Orange is not half size for everything. It is A+ only.
wrong.Neither; Orange bans all buys: Orange is not a ban on buying. It takes A+ setups, so the A+ gap pop is fine and the B pop waits.

questions.simple: Buy only the A+ gap pop, because an Orange market takes only A+ setups and the B pop waits.

reasons: the market reading is the owner's rulebook (F65)

questions.q: What now?
choices: The stop stays; it is the exit
Lower the stop for more room
questions.answer: The stop stays; it is the exit
questions.why: The stop stays. A close back under the pop day's low means the pop failed. The stop is just under that low anyway, so it is already doing its job. Breakeven comes later, between 2R and 5R, at the first trim.
questions.lesson_line: When the pop fails, the stop is already where it needs to be. Leave it.

wrong.Lower the stop for more room: Our stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Buy more near the stop: No adding. We take the full size at one price with one stop.
wrong.Raise the stop to breakeven: Our default moves the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim. A stop at 40.00 sits above today's close of 39.15 and would fire at once.

questions.story: You bought a pop at 40.00, stop 39.10. Two days later it closes at 39.15, under the pop day's low and five cents over your stop.
questions.simple: Leave the stop where it is, because it sits just under the pop day's low and only ever moves up.

reasons: the stop rule is the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.q: A $14 stock averages 1,600,000 shares a day over 50 days. How many dollars a day is that, in millions?
questions.why: $22.4 million. Dollars a day are price times shares: 14 x 1,600,000 / 1,000,000 = 22.4 million. We need $10 or more and at least $20 million a day on the 50-day average. This stock clears both tests, so it is on the list.
questions.lesson_line: Price times shares is the dollars. Twenty million a day or it is not on the list.
questions.simple: $22.4 million, which is price times shares and clears the $20 million a day we need.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook B23

wrong.$224 million: A decimal slip. That is ten times too big.
wrong.$0.11 million: Divided the shares by the price instead of multiplying.
wrong.$1,120 million: Multiplied by the 50 days of the average. The 50 days only set the average.

questions.q: What kind of loss was it?
choices: A planned loss, the plan working
A mistake: stop was too wide
Proof the setup does not work
questions.answer: A planned loss, the plan working
questions.why: A planned loss. The honest stop was 4.7% below the fill. That is past the 3.5% we call good, but inside the 5% we accept, so you took it smaller. The pop closed near its high on 1.24 times the base days' volume. The stop did its job.
questions.lesson_line: A wide stop is a reason for a small size. The loss stays small too.

wrong.A mistake: stop was too wide: Up to 5% is acceptable, and you took the smaller position. A wide stop is not banned.
wrong.A sign to widen stops: A stop never moves wider, and a wide honest stop already means a smaller size.
wrong.Proof the setup does not work: One loss at the stop proves nothing about the setup. A valid pop can fail, and then the stop does its job.

questions.story: Bought on the pop at 209.81 with the stop at 199.95. A 13-day base after a 41% decline. The pop closes near the high, on 1.24x the base days' volume. The honest stop is 4.7% below your fill. You took it smaller. Day 2 takes the stop.
questions.simple: A planned loss, because the wide stop was still acceptable, you sized down, and the stop did its job.

deeper.trap: Trap: calling the loss a mistake because it came on day 2. COIN, 2024-08-23, closed near the high with a 4.7% stop and was stopped on day 2. All four failed pops in our table closed strong, so the candle could not have warned you.

reasons: held decision D-006 on the volume gate
the cold check held it as a fix on D-006

questions.q: What do you do now?
choices: Take the loss; wait for a trigger
Buy it back at the next day's open
Widen the stop on the next trade
Avoid this stock for a month
questions.answer: Take the loss; wait for a trigger
questions.why: Take the loss and wait for a new trigger. A valid pop that failed; the stop did its job. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. No buying it back at once, no wider stop next time, and no ban on the stock.
questions.lesson_line: Some good pops fail. The stop keeps the cost small, and the next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.Buy it back at the next day's open: No new trigger, no new trade. After a stop-out we buy again only on a new trigger.
wrong.Widen the stop on the next trade: The stop only moves up, never wider. A wider stop only makes the next loss bigger.
wrong.Avoid this stock for a month: There is no ban. A new trigger is a new trade, up to 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock.

questions.story: A 29% decline, an 11-day base, then a gap open at 184.95 on 1.86x the base days' volume, closing high in its range. You bought the open with the stop at 182.70. The next session's low takes it.
questions.simple: Take the loss and wait, because we buy this stock again only when the setup triggers again as a fresh trade.

deeper.example: PLTR, 2025-12-10: buy 184.95, stop 182.70. The next session's low of 180.21 took the stop. A valid pop that failed, and the stop did its job. All four pop days in our failed examples closed strong, so the candle gave no warning. The loss was the size we planned.

reasons: re-entry after a stop-out is the owner's rulebook (B21)
the stop default is held (D-008)

questions.q: By our default rules, what happened?
questions.why: Stopped at 83.15, a planned loss. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. At 1.5R the stop had not moved. On day 3 the low of 81.50 went through 83.15.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the plan. A loss at the stop is the plan working.

wrong.Stopped at breakeven, 84.88: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. At 1.5R the stop had not moved.
wrong.Stopped at 81.50, the low: The stop sat at 83.15, so that was the planned exit. The day's low is only how far price ran after it.
wrong.Sold a third at 1.5R, held: We very rarely sell this early. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third.

questions.story: Bought the pop at 84.88, stop 83.15. It reaches 1.5R in two sessions, before any trim. On day 3 it trades down through the stop, to 81.50.
questions.simple: It was stopped at 83.15 as planned, because breakeven only starts at 2R and the trade got to 1.5R.

deeper.trap: The tempting move is to raise the stop once the trade is up. The card allows breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R. At 1.5R it is too early. A gap through the stop would bring in the gap rule instead.

reasons: the breakeven range comes from the card
the dossier and the card differ on breakeven here

questions.q: Bought at 60.00, stop 59.00. It gaps down; the first 30-minute low is 57.30. How many R would a stop there lose?
questions.why: 2.7R. One R is the buy minus the stop: 60.00 - 59.00. The loss at a stop of 57.30 is 60.00 - 57.30. So (60.00 - 57.30) / (60.00 - 59.00) = 2.7R. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop. There is a ceiling: if that takes the loss past 2R, get out.
questions.lesson_line: On a gap, the first 30 minutes decide. Past 2R, I am out.
questions.simple: 2.7R, which is past the 2R ceiling, so we get out.

deeper.trap: Trap: treating the first 30-minute low as a safe new stop. It is the new stop only while the loss stays within 2R. Here it would be 2.7R, so the answer is to get out, not to wait.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook B20

wrong.1.7R: Measured the fall from the stop, not from the fill.
wrong.2.0R: That is the ceiling, not the loss. The loss at 57.30 is bigger.
wrong.0.4R: Flipped the division: one R over the loss.

questions.q: Add to it here?
choices: No, a new trade if anything
questions.answer: No, a new trade if anything
questions.why: No adds. The full size at one price with one stop. The first pullback after the pop is the EMA Crossback, a separate setup and a new trade, not an add.
questions.lesson_line: The pop is one trade. The crossback, if it comes, is another.

wrong.Yes, add a third: Kell adds as each new range breaks. Our rule is one entry and no adding.
wrong.Yes, average up to full: The full size went on at the pop. Nothing is added on the way up.

questions.story: You hold a pop. It runs a few days, then pulls back into the rising averages and holds them.

questions.q: Weeks after the pop, you still hold part of the position. The stock runs far above its averages in a climax. What do we do?
choices: Sell a big part into the run
Sell it all at first sign
Add more, it is strong now
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the run
questions.why: Sell a big part into the run. A climax run on your own long is where we sell a big part, and it is a judgment call. Our card calls it an Exhaustion Extension, a climax run far above the averages. The trail stays on for the rest.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into the climax. The averages need time to catch up.

wrong.Sell it all at first sign: Our rule is a big part, not all. The rest stays on the trail.
wrong.Add more, it is strong now: No adding. We take the full size at one price with one stop.
wrong.Hold it; the trail decides: The trail sells on a close under the 9 EMA or 20 EMA. In a climax the stock sits far above it, so the trail would act only after the top.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into the climax, because a run far above the averages is where we take profits by hand.

deeper.trap: Why not let the trail decide? The trail is a close under the 9 EMA for fast movers, or the 20 EMA for steadier ones. In a climax the stock sits far above that average, so the trail would act only well after the top. We sell a big part by hand into the strength, then let the trail handle the rest.

reasons: the climax sale is the owner's rulebook (C34), a judgment call

questions.q: What do you do about the first sell?
choices: Judge it; 3R is not a sell order
Wait for the close to confirm 3R
questions.answer: Judge it; 3R is not a sell order
questions.why: Judge it. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. Trading through 3R is a reason to look, not a sell order.
questions.lesson_line: Trading through 3R is not a sell order. Judge the first sell.

wrong.Sell the whole position: Nothing says reaching 3R means selling it all. The first sell is a judgment.
wrong.Wait for the close to confirm 3R: A close does not make 3R a rule. The first sell is a judgment.
wrong.Take the 3R trim right away: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.

questions.story: Bought on the pop at 36.50 with the stop at 35.59, so 3R is 39.23. On day 2 the stock trades up through 3R.
questions.simple: Judge it. Trading through 3R is not an automatic sell, and we rarely sell this early.

deeper.trap: Trap: treating 3R as a sell trigger. The first sell depends on a variety of factors, such as how many days the push has run.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (the first sell is a judgment)

questions.q: Kell says to stay defensive in stocks when the index makes a Reversal Extension.
questions.why: False. Kell says to get aggressive trading individual stocks when you see a Reversal Extension on the index. Deepvue says the same of him: at market turning points he trades more aggressively and holds positions longer. For us, the market reading still guides how much risk we take.
questions.lesson_line: Kell watches the index first. When it shows a Reversal Extension, he gets aggressive in stocks.
questions.simple: False. Kell gets aggressive in stocks when the index makes a Reversal Extension, because that marks a market turning point.

deeper.counter: The same Kell sat out when no turn had come. On another occasion he wrote that he was avoiding long swings until he saw a major capitulation reversal extension in the QQQ or a switch to a buy signal.

reasons: market timing is a held decision, D-018

questions.q: What does our card say about this one?
choices: B- at best: smaller or pass
Normal size, the stop is honest
questions.answer: B- at best: smaller or pass
questions.why: B- at best. A stop that has to be 8% or more away is B- at best; take a smaller position or skip, never tighten it to fit. CRWD in March 2021 popped on 3 times the 50-day volume, left a stop 8.6% below the fill, and was stopped the next session at 47.40. Big volume does not fix a wide stop.
questions.lesson_line: A huge day can leave a huge stop. The size has to shrink to match it.

wrong.Pull the stop in to 3%: Never tighten the stop to fit. A stop inside the day's range is just a guess.
wrong.A+, the volume is huge: Volume does not fix the stop. A stop 8% or more away is B- at best.
wrong.Normal size, the stop is honest: An honest stop is the right stop, but it does not make a wide one fit. Wider than about 3% means a smaller position or a pass.

questions.story: A pop on 3 times the 50-day volume. The day's range is so wide that the stop sits 8.6% below the fill.
questions.simple: B- at best, because a stop 8% or more away is too wide, so we shrink the size or pass.

deeper.trap: A big day is not a good setup by itself. The wider the pop day's range, the farther the stop under its low sits from the fill. CRWD's range left a stop 8.6% away, and the pop was stopped the next session. With a stop that far, shrink the size or skip it. Never move the stop in to fit the size.

reasons: the 8% line is on the proposed card and the 3% line in the owner's rulebook (A13)
the example sits near a held decision (D-025)

questions.q: Where was the buy?
questions.why: As it traded through 30.24. We buy with a market order as price trades through the pivot. The close at 31.72 was 4.9% over the pivot, past the 4% chase line, so at the close it was a chase. SLB in January 2022 is the card's example of a pop buyable only as it traded through.
questions.lesson_line: Have the alert at the pivot. The buy is the trade through, not the close.

wrong.When it closed at 31.72: 31.72 is 4.9% over the pivot, past the 4% chase line.
wrong.At the next session's open: The close was already past the 4% chase line. After that we wait for a tight day or a pullback, not the next open.
wrong.A limit buy resting at 30.24: Entries are market orders. Our buy is a market order as price trades through the pivot.

questions.story: The chart ends the day before. One wide bar runs from inside the base through the pivot, 30.24, and both averages. It closes at 31.72, 4.9% over the pivot.
questions.simple: Buy with a market order as it trades through 30.24, because the close at 31.72 was past the 4% chase line.

deeper.trap: Why not wait for the close to be sure? The close is known only at the close, and a wide bar can run well past the chase line by then. Here it closed 4.9% over the pivot. So the buy is the trade through the pivot, set up with an alert at the pivot, not a decision at the bell.

reasons: market orders and the 4% line are the owner's rulebook (E57, C28)
trigger timing is a held decision (D-003)

questions.q: A stock is still falling hard, stretched far under its averages, on heavy volume. Is that the entry?
choices: Yes, with a stop at the low
No, buy after the first green day
questions.why: No. Buying the Reversal Extension low itself is bottom fishing, a named mistake. Kell says trading it is often best avoided. Wait for the price to consolidate under the averages as it forms a tradable pivot. The pop gives a clear pivot and a tighter stop.
questions.lesson_line: Let the low form, then let the base form. The pop is the buy, not the panic.

wrong.Yes, buy the capitulation: That is the named mistake of buying the low. The pivot forms later, as price settles under the averages.
wrong.Yes, with a stop at the low: The low is not in yet, so there is no low to put a stop under. The pop gives a clear pivot and a tighter stop.
wrong.No, buy after the first green day: One up day is still the window between the low and the pop, the hardest period to trade. Wait for the base and the pivot.

questions.simple: No. A stock still falling hard has no base or pivot yet, so buying now is bottom fishing.

deeper.trap: Trap: the panic feels like the best price. Kell's split is this: use the Reversal Extension to spot the bottom, then wait. The Wedge Pop is the better place to add exposure. The hardest period to trade is the window between the two.

reasons: whether a Reversal Extension must come first is a held decision, D-077

questions.q: Does the base still count as tight?
choices: Yes, the shakeout counts as tight
No, the ranges have not shrunk
No, an undercut breaks the base
Yes, but only once the ranges shrink
questions.answer: Yes, the shakeout counts as tight
questions.why: Yes. A shakeout also counts as tight. That is an undercut of the prior low by 1% that still closes up in the last 3 days. It is a second way into a tight base beside shrinking ranges, so this base counts.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout that closes up is the base clearing out sellers. It counts.

wrong.No, the ranges have not shrunk: Shrinking ranges is one way in. A shakeout that closes up is the other.
wrong.No, an undercut breaks the base: An undercut that closes up is the shakeout our card allows.
wrong.Yes, but only once the ranges shrink: The shakeout counts on its own. It is a second way in beside shrinking ranges, not an add-on.

questions.story: Inside the base, one day undercut the prior low by 1% and closed up. That was two days ago. The ranges have not shrunk.
questions.simple: Yes, a 1% undercut of the prior low that still closes up in the last 3 days counts as tight.

deeper.trap: A shakeout looks like a failure, because price breaks the prior low. Our card counts it only when the undercut is by 1% and the day still closes up, inside the last 3 days. An undercut that closes down is not a shakeout.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's shakeout line

questions.q: What do you do with the stop?
questions.why: Leave it. A real stop order with the broker. It only moves up, never down when the first days are weak.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an appointment, not a debate.

wrong.Lower it to 67.00: The stop never moves down. Weak first days are what it is there for.
wrong.Cancel it and watch: Every position has a real stop order with the broker.
wrong.Sell half, lower the rest: Lowering the stop on any part breaks the same rule.

questions.story: You bought a pop at 70.00, stop 68.50. Day 2 is weak and trades down to 68.70. It feels like it needs room.

questions.q: After three stop-outs on one stock this week, a fourth try is still allowed this week.
questions.why: False. At most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. After three, the week is done for that name. Each try is a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week on one name. Each one is a new trade with every rule.
questions.simple: False, because we allow at most three tries a week on one stock, so after three stop-outs the week is done.

deeper.trap: Three is the most, not a goal. Each try needs its own fresh trigger, its own stop and every rule. The month has a cap too: 6 tries on the same stock.

reasons: the try limits are the owner's rulebook (E56)

questions.q: What fits our guide?
choices: Pass; leave the money in cash
Short it; the market is Red
Take it with full risk on
questions.answer: Pass; leave the money in cash
questions.why: Pass and leave the money in cash. Red means mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. This stock is above its 200-day, so a short is out too, and the clean pop waits. The reading is a guide.
questions.lesson_line: In a Red market the best trade is usually no trade.

wrong.Short it; the market is Red: We short only below the 200-day. This stock is above it, so the short is out too.
wrong.Take it with full risk on: Full risk is for a Green market. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Take it, smaller and fewer: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Red is mostly cash.

questions.story: The market reading is Red. A clean pop sets up in a stock above its 200-day.
questions.simple: Pass and stay in cash, because a Red market means mostly cash, so even a clean pop waits.

deeper.trap: The reading is a guide, not a hard cap. Red leans hard toward cash, plus shorts below the 200-day, so a clean long still waits. Green allows full risk and up to 10 positions; Yellow means smaller and fewer.

reasons: the market reading is the owner's rulebook (F65, D46)

questions.q: Which setup is it?
questions.why: An undercut and rally. A U&R reclaims one prior low and can fire from under the averages. This stock dipped under last week's low and closed back over it the same day. It is still under both averages, with no tight base. A Wedge Pop needs a tight base and a close above both averages.
questions.lesson_line: Under the averages and back over a low is a U&R. Over the averages out of a base is a pop.

wrong.A Wedge Pop breakout: A Wedge Pop needs a tight base and a close above both averages. This has neither.
wrong.An EMA Crossback pullback: A crossback is the first pullback into averages the stock already rides. This stock is still under its averages.
wrong.A remount of its averages: A remount retakes a line lost for 5 or more closes with one wide candle. This stock reclaimed a prior low and is still under both averages.

questions.story: Price dipped under last week's low, then closed back over it the same day. It is still under both averages. There was no tight base.
questions.simple: It is an undercut and rally: the stock won back a prior low while still under its averages, with no tight base.

deeper.trap: Four setups can look alike. An undercut and rally reclaims one prior low and can fire from under the averages. A Wedge Pop needs a tight base and a close above both averages. A crossback is the first pullback into averages the stock already rides. A remount retakes a lost line with one wide candle. Ask what the stock just did and where it sits against its averages.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's lookalike lines

questions.q: Which is it?
choices: A Wedge Drop at the averages
A Wedge Pop that has failed
A shakeout before the real pop
questions.answer: A Wedge Drop at the averages
questions.why: A Wedge Drop. Kell's Wedge Drop is a tight range up into the averages, then a break down through them. It follows an Exhaustion Extension, or sometimes a stall without one. A Wedge Pop coils under the averages and pops up through them.
questions.lesson_line: Same coil, opposite door. Where it closes tells you which.

wrong.An EMA Crossback that failed: A crossback is a pullback that holds rising averages. This one sits under falling averages and broke down.
wrong.A Wedge Pop that has failed: A failed pop first closes up through the averages, then falls back. This stock only rose up to them, then closed down through them.
wrong.A shakeout before the real pop: A shakeout undercuts a prior low and still closes up. This stock closed down through both averages.

questions.story: After a climax top and a drop, the stock coils up into its falling averages for a few tight days. Then it closes down through both of them.
questions.simple: A Wedge Drop. The stock coiled up into its falling averages and then broke down through them, the reverse of a pop.

deeper.trap: Trap: the same tight coil can end either way. Under the averages and then up through them is a Wedge Pop. Up into falling averages and then down through them is the Drop. Into an Exhaustion Extension we sell a big part of a long.

reasons: rests on the criteria card (house)

questions.q: Is this a Wedge Pop?
choices: No; too few closes under the 20 EMA
Yes; the 12-day base is long enough
Yes; an 18% dip is deep enough
No; a 12-day base is too long
questions.answer: No; too few closes under the 20 EMA
questions.why: No. A Wedge Pop comes from a correction that spent most of three weeks under the 20 EMA: our card wants at least 8 of the 15 closes before the pop under it. This stock had 7. It is a pullback inside an uptrend it already rides, not a rally back up through the averages from under them.
questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the 20 EMA before the pop. Too few, and it is a pullback, not a pop.

wrong.Yes; the 12-day base is long enough: Base length is not the gate here. The count of closes under the 20 EMA before the pop is, and it falls one short.
wrong.Yes; an 18% dip is deep enough: Depth is not what the card counts. It counts closes under the 20 EMA, and there were too few.
wrong.No; a 12-day base is too long: The card sets a minimum base, not a maximum. The base is not the problem.

questions.story: The day before a possible pop. An 18% dip into a 12-day base. Only 7 of the 15 closes before the pop sat under the 20 EMA.
questions.simple: No, because only 7 of the 15 closes before it sat under the 20 EMA, so this is a pullback in an uptrend.

deeper.trap: Trap: calling it a pop because the dip and the base look right. The count of closes under the 20 EMA is the test, and this stock fell one short, so it was a pullback in an uptrend.

reasons: the correction test is held (D-077), the key uses only the card's context line

questions.q: Two clean pops look alike. One follows real company news; the other has none. On our card, which grades higher?
choices: The one with news behind it
The one with no news at all
They tie, since news is priced in
Neither, only the chart grades it
questions.answer: The one with news behind it
questions.why: The one with the news behind it. Our card counts a catalyst behind the pop, real news, as an A+ cue. Grading is a judgment, so the cue tips the grade and does not decide it. The chart still comes first, and the other cues still count.
questions.lesson_line: A reason behind the move adds to the grade. The chart still comes first.

wrong.The one with no news at all: The card lists a real catalyst as an A+ cue. The pop without one has no such cue.
wrong.They tie, since news is priced in: A catalyst is a grade cue on our card. It lifts the pop that has one.
wrong.Neither, only the chart grades it: The chart comes first, but the card counts a real catalyst as an A+ cue, so the chart is not the only thing that grades a pop.

questions.simple: The pop with news behind it grades higher on our card, because a real reason behind the move is an A+ cue.

deeper.trap: Trap: a catalyst is a plus, not a free pass. The pop still needs the tight base and the pivot, and the other cues still count.

reasons: rests on the criteria card (house)

questions.q: What is the most you would risk on it?
questions.why: 1.5%, sized up for A+. An A+ setup risks 1% to 1.5%, and a Green market allows full risk per grade. 1.5% is the most any grade uses, and 2% is the absolute ceiling. The position cap can still shrink the shares.
questions.lesson_line: Grade sets the size. A+ in a Green market is where I lean in, inside the ceiling.

wrong.1%, normal size: 1% is the low end of the A+ band and the top of A and B. An A+ is sized up to 1.5%.
wrong.2%, the ceiling: 2% is the absolute ceiling for any trade, but 1.5% is the most any grade uses.
wrong.0.5%, sized down: Sizing down is for B- or lower. This one is A+.

questions.story: An A+ pop in a Green market: a gap through the pivot after the index's own low, on heavy volume.
questions.simple: An A+ pop in a Green market can risk up to 1.5% and is sized up. Two percent is the ceiling for any trade.

deeper.trap: Trap: reading 1.5% as the number to use. The risk is a band by grade, and under 1% is normal. The share count is the smaller of the risk-based size and the position cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E49 and A1
fixed at the cold check

questions.q: The day before a possible pop. Is this a Wedge Pop base to watch?
choices: Watch it; the bars are tightening
Skip it; the base looks loose
Skip it; it sits above the averages
Buy it now, ahead of the pop
questions.answer: Watch it; the bars are tightening
questions.why: Watch it; the bars are tightening. This base ran two weeks of shrinking bars under both averages, a contraction of 0.44, the tightest of our ten examples. The card's line is under 0.85. The next day it popped above the pivot and both averages.
questions.lesson_line: Small bars under the averages are the coil. The pop is the release.

wrong.Skip it; the base looks loose: The ranges shrank to 0.44 times the 10 before, the tightest of our ten examples. That is not loose.
wrong.Skip it; it sits above the averages: This base sat under both averages for two weeks, which is where a pop comes from.
wrong.Buy it now, ahead of the pop: Buying inside the wedge before the pop is a named mistake. We buy as it trades through the pivot.

questions.simple: Watch it, because the bars shrink into the right edge under both averages, which is the coil before a pop.

deeper.example: The tight test on our card: the last 5 sessions' average range under 0.85 times the 10 before them. This base measured 0.44, so the bars shrank hard into the pivot. Smaller is tighter. A watch is not a buy: the buy comes only as it trades through the pivot.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's tight test

questions.q: The day before a possible pop. Is this a Wedge Pop base to watch?
choices: Skip it; the bars are not tight
Watch it; it sits under its averages
Watch it; wide bars show strength
Buy it now, ahead of the pop
questions.answer: Skip it; the bars are not tight
questions.why: Skip it. The last 5 sessions' ranges were 1.11 times the 10 before them, and the card wants under 0.85 times. A wide, loose rebound through the averages is a remount, not a Wedge Pop.
questions.lesson_line: A rebound with big bars is not a coil. No tightening, no pop.

wrong.Watch it; it sits under its averages: Being under the averages is only part of it. The base must also tighten, and the card wants under 0.85 times.
wrong.Watch it; wide bars show strength: Wide bars are a loose rebound, not a coil. A rebound like this is a remount, not a Wedge Pop.
wrong.Buy it now, ahead of the pop: Buying inside the base before the pop is a named mistake. We buy as it trades through the pivot.

questions.simple: Skip it, because the recent bars were not smaller than the earlier ones, so this is a loose rebound, not a coil.

deeper.counter: A place under the averages is only one of the tests. The base must also tighten, with ranges shrinking. A rebound on wide bars through the averages is a remount, a separate setup that needs no tight base. In our example it reached 2.68R at best and was stopped.

reasons: rests on the proposed card's tight test

questions.q: Where does the stop live?
questions.story: You buy the pop at 50.00. The pop day's low is 48.80. You are about to sit in a two-hour meeting and cannot watch the screen.
choices: A real stop order with the broker
A phone alert set at the stop price
A mental stop you promise to follow
Place it after the meeting ends
questions.answer: A real stop order with the broker
questions.why: A real stop order with the broker. Every position has one, not a stop kept in your head. The order goes in when you buy, so the meeting leaves nothing unprotected. The stop sits a few cents under 48.80 and only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: No stop order, no position. The stop lives with the broker.

wrong.A phone alert set at the stop price: An alert only tells you. It is not a stop order with the broker.
wrong.A mental stop you promise to follow: A stop kept in your head is not a stop. It needs a real order.
wrong.Place it after the meeting ends: The meeting is the unprotected stretch. The order goes in when you buy.

questions.simple: A real stop order with the broker, because an alert or a promise cannot sell for you while you are away.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D41

questions.q: Weak first days after the pop are no reason to lower the stop.
questions.why: True. The stop is a real order with the broker that only moves up, never down, when the first days are weak. Weak first days are exactly what the stop is there for.
questions.lesson_line: A stop moves up or stays. A weak start never moves it down.
questions.simple: True, because a weak start is exactly why the stop exists, and it only ever moves up.

reasons: the stop rule is the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: A Wedge Pop long on a stock needs the pop day to close above the 200-day simple moving average.
questions.why: True. For a stock, we take no longs below the 200-day simple moving average. The one exception is indexes and ETFs built to magnify an index's moves, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. About half of all pops come under it and are not ours.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day or it is not our pop, however clean the base.
questions.simple: True, because our hard rule bars stock longs below the 200-day line.

reasons: the 200-day rule is the owner's settled rulebook line (B26)

questions.q: Our card checks the index before a Wedge Pop buy. Which index reading fails that check?
choices: Falling EMAs and a new 20-session low
Rising EMAs off a fresh 20-session low
One down day on volume above average
questions.answer: Falling EMAs and a new 20-session low
questions.why: Falling EMAs and a new 20-session low. Our card compares the index's short averages with 5 sessions ago. It also looks for a new 20-session low in the last 5 sessions. Both together mean the index is still making lower lows with its averages falling.
questions.lesson_line: Before the buy, check the index: falling short averages plus a fresh 20-session low means it is still falling.

wrong.The index closing under its 200-day: The card's index test does not use the 200-day. It reads the short averages and a new 20-session low.
wrong.Rising EMAs off a fresh 20-session low: Rising averages pass the check. The card flags the index only when its averages fall and a new low prints.
wrong.One down day on volume above average: One heavy down day is not the test. The card compares the averages with 5 sessions ago and looks for a 20-session low.

questions.simple: Our card calls the index still falling when its short averages fell over 5 sessions and it hit a new 20-session low in that span.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line whose numbers are the card's own reading; the dossier gives the words, not the numbers
the card lists a falling index both as a no-buy invalidation and as a B- cue, so this item keys only the test, never the outcome

questions.story: A stock bottomed on Monday after a sharp decline. On Tuesday and Wednesday it closed tight under its 10 and 20-day EMAs. Thursday it gapped above both averages and above those two days' highs, and closed above both.
questions.q: Is Thursday a Wedge Pop buy by our card?
choices: No; the base ran only 2 sessions
Yes; a gap over the pivot is an A+ pop
Yes; it closed above both averages
No; a base needs at least 10 sessions
questions.answer: No; the base ran only 2 sessions
questions.why: No. The base needs at least 3 sessions after the low, with at least half the closes at or under the higher average. This one ran only 2, Tuesday and Wednesday. TraderLion: no lasting bottom until the stock tests the averages and has a few days to retreat. Without the base this is a rebound, not a Wedge Pop. Buying in the window before the base is built is a named mistake.
questions.simple: No, because the base needs at least three sessions after the low, and this one ran only two.
questions.lesson_line: Count the base. Fewer than three sessions after the low is a rebound, not a pop.

wrong.Yes; a gap over the pivot is an A+ pop: A gap through the pivot and the averages is the A+ pop, but only once the base is built. Two sessions are too few.
wrong.Yes; it closed above both averages: A close above both averages is a cross. A cross alone is not a Wedge Pop, because it needs the tight base first.
wrong.No; a base needs at least 10 sessions: The card needs at least 3 sessions after the low, not 10. A few days to retreat is enough.
